description: StrainWatch ranks roads, rail lines, pipelines and canals by how unevenly the ground beneath them is sinking, using NASA OPERA and NISAR radar. Solo entry; the team is complete.
summary: Radar satellites measure how fast land sinks. The damage happens where it sinks unevenly: that is where roads crack, pipelines bend and earth fissures open. StrainWatch takes any road, rail line, pipeline or canal and ranks every 300 m of it by how unevenly the ground beneath is sinking, using ten years of NASA OPERA DISP-S1 radar and the first year of NISAR. A county road engineer gets a ranked list, ten inspection stops and a printable sheet for each. It covers 120 places in 47 US states, Mexico and India. Every place is compared with ground measurements where they exist, and the tests that failed are shown beside the ones that held.
details:
THE QUESTION

A county has thousands of kilometres of road and one field crew. Where should the crew go first?

WHAT IT DOES

Pick a place, or draw or upload your own line. StrainWatch cuts it into pieces of about 300 m and ranks each piece by how unevenly the ground under it is sinking. The top 5% is marked "Inspect first", the next 15% "Watch". Ground the radar could not read is marked "Not observed" and is never shown as stable. The Inspection Planner turns the ranking into a short list of stops, and each stop prints as a one-page sheet with a map, the sinking history and what to look for. The list also downloads as CSV or GeoJSON for the GIS an agency already runs.

WHO IT IS FOR

A county road engineer choosing which roads to check; a pipeline, canal, rail or power-line operator checking their own line; a state geological survey deciding where to map fissures next.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Rate: a straight-line fit through ten years of radar dates at every pixel (NASA OPERA DISP-S1, 2016 to 2026).

2. Smooth: 90 m cells, then the median of each 3 x 3 block, giving a 270 m grid.

3. Unevenness: how much the sinking rate changes per kilometre (mm/yr per km).

4. Rank: each cell against the rest of its radar window.

5. Line: each 300 m piece takes the highest unevenness under it.

The app is a folder of static files. There is no server and no licence fee; all scoring runs in the browser. A county or state GIS office could host it and rerun one script when NASA publishes new radar.

HOW NISAR IS USED

NISAR L2 GUNW pairs are stacked at 116 of the 120 places and shown beside Sentinel-1 with a compare slider. At Mexico City one year of NISAR matches ten years of Sentinel-1 (r = 0.94 on 286,000 pixels). At the 22 places where Sentinel-1 reads less than half the ground, NISAR keeps a usable signal on 71% against 36%. At 109 places the ground moves too little for a one-year NISAR record to add anything yet, and the app says so. In Chennai, outside the OPERA coverage, StrainWatch has only 3.5 months of NISAR: it reports that sinking there is not detectable yet and shows how long a record is needed.

WHAT WE TESTED, AND WHAT FAILED

- Willcox Basin, Arizona: radar against 38 survey benchmarks, rank correlation 0.85.

- Willcox forward test: using only radar from before 2023, scored on fissures mapped afterwards. Unevenness scored 0.90 (AUC); sinking rate alone scored 0.75. It did NOT beat "look near fissures already mapped" (0.92). StrainWatch ranks ground for inspection. It does not predict where a fissure will open.

- Mexico City: radar against 9 GPS stations, r = 0.98, error 17 mm/yr. One station is off by about 50 mm/yr.

- Phoenix East Valley: 26 survey benchmarks, rank correlation 0.90.

- The other 116 places against GPS (Nevada Geodetic Laboratory): 105 agree, 7 agree only weakly, 4 have no station. 51 of these checks rest on one or two stations, and the app says so at each one.

- 31 automated tests check the scoring maths and that the numbers on screen match the research tables.

WORKED EXAMPLE

In the Willcox Basin, 3,759 km of road become 154 km to look at first, and then ten stops.

LIMITS

This is a relative screening index. It is not a damage assessment, an engineering finding or a forecast. The processed windows cover about 1.7% of lower-48 land area; everywhere else is "not processed yet". At 85 places the signal is weak and the app says nothing stands out. Nobody outside the team has used it yet: the next step is one field day with a county crew on the ten Willcox stops, recording what they find, including "nothing".

BUILT WITH

JavaScript (MapLibre GL, D3), Python (NumPy, rasterio, h5py) for the data build, Node for tests, GitHub Pages for hosting. Code: https://github.com/neric-joel/strainwatch

USE OF AI

AI coding assistants (Anthropic's Claude) were used in building the website: the web app and the data scripts behind it, written under the team's direction. No AI runs inside the app: the ranking and the planner are plain arithmetic. There are no AI-generated images, audio or video; the demo video is a screen capture of the app narrated by a team member.
